CausalChain: MALAT1 relies on its triple helix structure for stability -> Small molecules (e.g., diphenyl furan derivatives) can specifically bind to this triple helix -> Binding disrupts critical lncRNA–protein interactions (such as with chromatin modifiers like EZH2) -> Disruption leads to altered chromatin states and reprogramming of tumor metabolism -> Metabolic shifts reduce chemoresistance and enhance anti-tumor immune responses
Hypothesis: Targeting the triple helix structure of oncogenic lncRNAs like MALAT1 with specific small-molecule modulators will reprogram tumor metabolism and reduce drug resistance, thereby enhancing the anti-tumor immune response in aggressive cancers.
Abstract: We propose that the stability-conferring triple helix structures in oncogenic long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), such as MALAT1, represent an untapped target for small-molecule modulators. Binding of precisely designed ligands to these structures may induce conformational remodeling that disrupts lncRNA–protein interactions, thereby reprogramming tumor cell metabolism and reducing chemoresistance. This novel intervention could also create a more immunogenic tumor microenvironment, paving the way for synergistic cancer therapies. Our hypothesis integrates structural targeting with downstream functional shifts, offering a new modality in lncRNA-based precision medicine.
